Healing Outdoors: How Nature Helps Us Process Loss

Grief reshapes both mind and body — and increasingly, researchers argue that time spent in natural surroundings can ease this profound transition.

VIVID IELTS Reading Editorial · 6 min read

Losing someone close to us is one of the most disorienting experiences a person can face. Grief does not simply sit in the mind; it rewires the brain's expectations, forcing it to adjust to an absence where a familiar presence once was. Psychologists describe this as a slow, often painful recalibration that can take years to complete, as the bereaved learn to hold both continued love and permanent loss at the same time.

The effects of grief are not confined to our emotions. Studies consistently show that intense loss places measurable strain on the cardiovascular system, elevating heart rate and blood pressure while increasing susceptibility to inflammation and chronic illness. Close relationships appear to act as a buffer against everyday stress; once that buffer disappears, the body becomes more exposed to the physiological consequences of hardship, flooding it with stress hormones that can compromise both heart and immune function over time.

Despite this, many workplaces, schools and even families remain poorly equipped to support people through bereavement. A widely cited theory suggests that grief unfolds in a fixed sequence of stages leading to a tidy resolution. In practice, however, most researchers now agree that grief is far more circular than linear, resurfacing unpredictably rather than progressing neatly toward closure. Expecting mourners to "move on" according to a set timetable can add unnecessary pressure to an already difficult process.

This is where the natural world may offer a valuable, if underused, form of support. Spending time outdoors removes some of the intrusive demands of modern, indoor life and creates space for mindfulness — a state of calm, present-moment awareness that many find hard to access amid daily routines. Natural environments provide a kind of solitude that invites contemplation without isolation, along with ambient, restorative sounds that can gently redirect attention away from rumination and toward something larger than one's own loss.

While dedicated research into nature-based grief support is still limited, a substantial body of evidence already links exposure to green spaces with measurable physiological benefits: lower blood pressure, reduced stress-hormone production, decreased inflammation and a lower long-term risk of heart disease. Given how directly these outcomes mirror the physical toll of bereavement, pairing grief support with time in nature seems less like a coincidence and more like common sense.

None of this suggests that grief is a medical condition requiring treatment, nor that nature can replace professional or communal support. But because loss is such a universal part of the human experience, learning to sit with it — outdoors, unhurried, and without judgement — may be one of the simplest tools available for helping people carry it forward.
